name: The Culminating Point of Victory
statement: An offensive can be pushed past the point where its strength is spent, turning victory into defeat.
statementAccent: past the point where its strength is spent
meaning: The culminating point is the moment in a military offensive at which the attacker's strength no longer exceeds the defender's, when an advancing force's offensive power is spent so that continuing no longer yields advantage and instead exposes it to overextension, exhaustion, and counterattack. Clausewitz distinguished the culminating point of the attack, where the advance can no longer physically continue, from the broader culminating point of victory, the point beyond which pressing on brings diminishing or negative returns and a hard-won advantage can be squandered, turning victory into defeat.
mechanism: The core insight is asymmetric: the attacker tends to weaken as it advances while the defender may strengthen. Attrition and casualties consume the attacker; supply lines lengthen and grow vulnerable; captured territory, fortresses, and hostile populations must be garrisoned, drawing troops from the spearhead; fatigue and friction accumulate. Meanwhile the defender, falling back toward its own base, shortens its supply lines, draws on fresh reserves, gains local support, and recovers morale. The attack culminates where the attacker's declining strength meets the defender's rising strength, and to press beyond that is, in Clausewitz's phrase, a destructive step that causes reaction.

examples.text: The concept grew from Clausewitz's study of the 1812 invasion: the Grande Armee reached Moscow but could not compel peace, having likely passed its culminating point well before, and the retreat became a catastrophe.

Ludendorff's offensives broke through dramatically but created deep, vulnerable salients, outran their logistics, and exhausted their irreplaceable assault divisions just as fresh American troops arrived, a textbook overreach followed by the Allied counteroffensive.
Modern doctrine defines the culminating point as where a force can no longer continue its form of operation, offence or defence, making it a central element of operational planning.

variants.name: Attack versus victory
variants.text: The culminating point of the attack, whether the advance can physically continue, and the culminating point of victory, whether it has become strategically self-defeating to continue, two distinct thresholds.

variants.name: The defensive culminating point
variants.text: The corresponding point at which a defender can no longer mount counteroffensive action, showing culmination applies to both attacker and defender.

whyItMatters: Identifying the anticipated culminating point tells a commander how far an offensive can realistically reach and when to plan a halt, an operational pause, consolidation, or a transition to defence, before the force overextends. The concept survives in modern doctrine under the term culmination, treated as a central element of operational design at tactical, operational, and strategic levels, so that the attacker aims to reach its objective before culminating and the defender aims to force the attacker to culminate short of it.

working.text: track how the attacker weakens with distance while the defender strengthens on interior lines, and locate where they cross.
set the offensive's reach so it stops, consolidates, or turns to defence before it overextends past its culminating point.
distinguish whether an advance can physically continue from whether continuing has become strategically self-defeating.

limits: The culminating point is clearest in hindsight and very hard to fix in real time, since commanders rarely know they have passed it until the reaction sets in. Because it depends on many shifting variables, attrition rates, logistics, enemy reserves, morale, weather, and political will, it is an estimate and a warning, not a precise, calculable coordinate. It is a principle of judgement that resists reduction to a formula, and the historical culmination points of famous campaigns are debated by historians rather than settled facts.
misreadings: The culminating point is not the high-water mark or peak of victory; colloquially culmination suggests a climax of success, but in Clausewitz's sense it is the point of maximum sustainable advantage beyond which strength declines, a warning threshold. The culminating point of the attack is not identical to the culminating point of victory. It does not mean merely running out of fuel or ammunition; it is a net balance of forces including attrition, garrison burdens, morale, and the defender's recovery. And it applies to the defender as well as the attacker.
origin: Set out by Carl von Clausewitz in 'On War' (1832), Book Seven, which treats the culminating point of the attack and, separately, the culminating point of victory; the concept grew from his study of Napoleon's 1812 invasion of Russia.

sources.text: Clausewitz, On War, Book 7, Chapter 22, 'On the Culminating Point of Victory' (Graham translation, ClausewitzStudies.org). — the strategic threshold and its reaction.
